definition: The function $X(z) = \sum_n x[n] z^{-n}$ of a complex variable $z$ that packs a discrete-time signal $x[n]$ into one function on the complex plane.
The set of points $z$ where the z-transform sum converges absolutely. It is a ring $r_{in} < |z| < r_{out}$ bounded by poles, and together with the formula $X(z)$ it fixes the signal.
The complex plane of the variable $z$ of a z-transform. A point $z = \rho e^{j\omega}$ weights sample $n$ by $\rho^{-n} e^{-j\omega n}$.
The circle $|z| = 1$ in the complex plane. On it $z = e^{j\omega}$, and a z-transform becomes the discrete-time Fourier transform.

A point where a z-transform is infinite: a root of the denominator of a rational $X(z)$. The surface $|X(z)|$ shoots up there; a pole at $r e^{j\theta}$ in a causal signal means a term $r^n e^{j\theta n}$ in time.
A point where a z-transform is 0: a root of the numerator of a rational $X(z)$. A zero on the unit circle blocks that frequency completely.
$X(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_n x[n] e^{-j\omega n}$: the z-transform on the unit circle. It exists as an ordinary sum when the unit circle lies inside the region of convergence.
How strongly, and with what phase shift, a linear system passes a sinusoid of each frequency. For a discrete-time system it is $H(e^{j\omega})$, the transfer function on the unit circle.
A signal that is zero for $n < 0$, or a system whose impulse response is. Its region of convergence is the outside of a circle, including $z = \infty$.

A system is BIBO stable when every bounded input gives a bounded output, which holds exactly when $\sum_n |h[n]| < \infty$: the unit circle lies in the region of convergence. A causal system is stable when all its poles are inside the unit circle.
A signal that is zero before some time $n_0$. Its region of convergence is the outside of its outermost pole.
A signal that is zero after some time $n_0$. Its region of convergence is the inside of its innermost pole.
A signal that runs forever in both directions of time. Its region of convergence, if any, is a ring between two poles.
The signal $\delta[n]$: 1 at $n = 0$ and 0 everywhere else. Its z-transform is 1.
The signal $u[n]$: 1 for $n \ge 0$ and 0 before. Its z-transform is $1/(1 - z^{-1})$ for $|z| > 1$.
Getting $x[n]$ back from $X(z)$ and its region of convergence, by partial fractions, long division, or the contour integral $x[n] = \frac{1}{2\pi j}\oint X(z) z^{n-1} dz$ round a circle in the ROC.
Splitting a rational function into a sum of simple pieces, one per pole, so each can be inverted on its own.
A filter that removes one narrow band of frequencies. In discrete time, zeros on the unit circle at $\pm\theta$ block the frequency $\omega = \theta$ completely.
Reading $|X(z)|$ at a point as the gain times the product of the distances to the zeros divided by the product of the distances to the poles.
The output $h[n]$ of a linear time-invariant system when the input is the unit impulse. Its z-transform is the system's transfer function.

The function $X(s) = \int x(t)\, e^{-st}\, dt$ of a complex variable $s = \sigma + j\omega$ that packs a continuous-time signal $x(t)$ into one function on the complex plane. On the line $s = j\omega$ it becomes the Fourier transform.

The complex plane of the variable $s = \sigma + j\omega$ of a Laplace transform, with $\sigma$ across and $j\omega$ up. A point $s$ weights the signal at time $t$ by $e^{-st}$, an arrow that turns at $\omega$ and grows or shrinks at rate $\sigma$.

A point where a Laplace transform is infinite: a root of the denominator of a rational $X(s)$. A pole at $p$ contributes a term $e^{pt}$ to the signal, so its distance left of the imaginary axis sets the decay rate and its height sets the oscillation frequency.
A point where a Laplace transform is 0: a root of the numerator of a rational $X(s)$. A zero on the imaginary axis blocks that frequency completely.

The set of $s$ for which the Laplace integral converges. It is a vertical strip $\alpha < \operatorname{Re} s < \beta$, because the size of $e^{-st}$ depends only on $\operatorname{Re} s$, and for a rational transform it is bounded by poles.

The ratio $H(s) = Y(s)/X(s)$ of the Laplace transforms of output and input of a linear time-invariant system that starts at rest. It is the transform of the impulse response, and its values on the imaginary axis give the frequency response.
The inversion formula $x(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi j}\int_{c-j\infty}^{c+j\infty} X(s)\,e^{st}\,ds$, taken up a vertical line $\operatorname{Re} s = c$ inside the region of convergence.

The signal $x(t)$ recovered from $X(s)$ and its region of convergence, usually by partial fractions and a table, or by the Bromwich integral. The same formula with a different region gives a different signal.
For a causal signal with no impulse at the origin, $x(0^+) = \lim_{s\to\infty} sX(s)$: the starting value is the far-away height of $sX(s)$.
If every pole of $sX(s)$ is strictly in the left half-plane, then $x(\infty) = \lim_{s\to 0} sX(s)$: the value the signal settles to.
Convolution in time becomes multiplication of transforms: $(x*y)(t) \leftrightarrow X(s)Y(s)$, with a region containing the intersection of the two regions. In decibels the two surfaces add.

The transform $\int_{0^-}^{\infty} x(t)e^{-st}dt$, started just before the switch-on so that initial conditions enter through $\mathcal{L}\{x'\} = sX(s) - x(0^-)$. It is the form used to solve differential equations.

The number $\zeta$ in $s^2 + 2\zeta\omega_n s + \omega_n^2$, equal to the cosine of the angle between a pole and the negative real axis. Below 1 the system oscillates; at 1 it is critically damped; above 1 it is overdamped.
The number $\omega_n$ in $s^2 + 2\zeta\omega_n s + \omega_n^2$: the distance of the poles from the origin, and the frequency at which the system would oscillate with no damping.
For a pole at $-a$, the time $1/a$ in which the signal $e^{-at}$ falls to $1/e = 0.368$ of its value. For an RC circuit it is the product $RC$.
The case $\zeta = 1$ of a second-order system, a double pole on the negative real axis: the fastest return to rest without oscillation.

A peak in the frequency response where the imaginary axis passes close to a pole pair. For the damped sine $\omega_0/((s+a)^2 + \omega_0^2)$, with poles at $-a \pm j\omega_0$ and $a$ small, its height is about $1/(2a)$, so halving the distance $a$ doubles the peak.
The part of the s-plane with $\operatorname{Re} s < 0$. A causal system is stable exactly when all its poles are in it; under $z = e^{sT}$ it maps inside the unit circle.
For a simple pole $p$ of $F(s)$, the number $\lim_{s\to p}(s-p)F(s)$. The Bromwich integral is a sum of residues of $X(s)e^{st}$ at the poles on one side of the line.

The function $X(f) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)\,e^{-j2\pi f t}\,dt$ that says how much of each frequency $f$ a signal $x(t)$ contains, and with what phase. The inverse transform rebuilds $x(t)$ from $X(f)$.

The representation of a signal that repeats every $T$ seconds as a sum of turning arrows at multiples of $1/T$: $x(t) = \sum_k c_k e^{j2\pi k t/T}$ with $c_k = \frac1T\int_0^T x(t)e^{-j2\pi k t/T}dt$.
One of the sinusoids in a Fourier series, with frequency $k/T$ for a whole number $k$. The first harmonic, $k = 1$, is the fundamental, whose period is the period of the signal itself.
A plot of the amplitude $|c_k|$ (or $A_k$) and the phase $\angle c_k$ of each frequency component of a signal against frequency. It describes the same signal as the waveform, in terms of frequency.

The complex number $Ae^{j\varphi}$ that holds the amplitude and phase of a sinusoid $A\cos(\omega t + \varphi) = \operatorname{Re}[Ae^{j\varphi}e^{j\omega t}]$, leaving out the time dependence. Sinusoids of one frequency add by adding their phasors.

The frequency of an arrow $e^{-j\omega t}$ that turns clockwise. A real signal contains arrows at $+f$ and $-f$ with complex-conjugate coefficients, so its spectrum is mirror-symmetric and the negative half adds no information.

The fact that $\int_0^T e^{j2\pi k t/T}e^{-j2\pi m t/T}dt$ is $T$ when $k = m$ and $0$ otherwise. It is why the Fourier coefficient integral isolates one frequency and why Parseval's theorem has no cross terms.

A phase that is a straight line in frequency, $\varphi(f) = -2\pi f t_0$. It is the signature of a pure delay of $t_0$ seconds: amplitudes are unchanged and each frequency is shifted by the same time.
The statement that a signal's average power (or energy) is the same whether computed from the waveform or from its spectrum. For a periodic signal, $\frac1T\int_0^T x^2\,dt = \sum_k |c_k|^2$.

The overshoot of about $8.95\%$ of the jump that a partial Fourier sum shows next to a discontinuity. Adding harmonics narrows the overshoot and moves it toward the jump but does not reduce its height.

The function $\operatorname{sinc}(u) = \sin(\pi u)/(\pi u)$, with $\operatorname{sinc}(0) = 1$ and zeros at the nonzero integers. It is the Fourier transform of a rectangular pulse: $\operatorname{rect}(t/\tau)\leftrightarrow\tau\operatorname{sinc}(f\tau)$.
The rule that a signal cannot be narrow in both time and frequency: with RMS widths $\sigma_t$ and $\sigma_f$, $\sigma_t\sigma_f \ge 1/(4\pi)$, with equality for the Gaussian pulse.
The effect by which, after sampling at rate $f_s$, a frequency $f$ above $f_s/2$ gives the same samples as the lower frequency $|f - mf_s|$ and so cannot be told apart from it.
Twice the highest frequency in a signal, $2f_{\max}$. Sampling faster than this keeps every frequency within $0$ to $f_s/2$ and avoids aliasing.
Half the sampling rate, $f_s/2$: the highest frequency a sampled signal can represent. Components above it fold back below it.

The map from $N$ samples $x[n]$ to $N$ numbers $X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]e^{-j2\pi kn/N}$, which are the DTFT sampled at $N$ equally spaced points round the unit circle. Bin $k$ stands for the frequency $kf_s/N$.
The spreading of a sinusoid's energy across many DFT bins when it does not complete a whole number of cycles in the window, because the repeated window then has a jump at each seam.

A smooth taper, such as the Hann window $0.5 - 0.5\cos(2\pi n/N)$, applied to the samples before a DFT so they approach zero at the ends. It lowers leakage far from the peak at the cost of a wider main lobe.

Any algorithm that computes the DFT in about $N\log_2 N$ operations rather than $N^2$. The radix-2 version splits the samples into even and odd halves repeatedly, and needs $\frac N2\log_2 N$ complex multiplications.
The unit complex number $W_N^k = e^{-j2\pi k/N}$ that multiplies one input of an FFT butterfly. Its key properties are $W_N^2 = W_{N/2}$ and $W_N^{k+N/2} = -W_N^k$.
The basic step of the radix-2 FFT: from inputs $a$ and $b$ it forms $a + Wb$ and $a - Wb$, using one multiplication for two outputs. Drawn with crossing lines, it looks like a butterfly.

The reordering of the input of an in-place radix-2 FFT so that sample $n$ sits at the position given by its index written in binary and read backwards. For $N = 8$, $x[1]$ goes to position 4 and $x[3]$ to 6.

The integral $y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau)\, h(t-\tau)\, d\tau$, written $y = x * h$: flip one function, slide it by $t$, multiply by the other and take the area. It gives the output of a linear, time-invariant system with impulse response $h$ for the input $x$.
The discrete form of convolution, $y[n] = \sum_k x[k]\, h[n-k]$. Two sequences of lengths $N$ and $M$ give $N + M - 1$ outputs; the sum is the same arithmetic as multiplying two polynomials.

A system that is linear (scaled and summed inputs give scaled and summed outputs) and time-invariant (a delayed input gives the same output, delayed). Its output is always the convolution of the input with its impulse response.

The rule $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau)\, \delta(t-\tau)\, d\tau = x(t)$: an impulse picks out one value of a function. It writes any signal as a sum of shifted, scaled impulses, and it makes $\delta$ the identity of convolution, $x * \delta = x$.

The continuous-time unit impulse $\delta(t)$: zero everywhere except at $t = 0$, with total area 1. It is not an ordinary function but is defined by what it does inside an integral (the sifting property).
The output of a system when the input is the unit step $u(t)$. For an LTI system it is $u * h$, the running integral of the impulse response: $s(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{t} h(\tau)\, d\tau$.
The property of a system that delaying the input by $T$ only delays the output by $T$, without changing its shape: the system behaves the same today as tomorrow.
Two systems one after the other. For LTI systems the overall impulse response is $h_1 * h_2$, and because convolution is associative and commutative the order of the two does not change the output.
The Fourier transform of a convolution is the product of the transforms: $\mathcal{F}\{x * h\} = X(f)\,H(f)$. Its dual says a product in time is a convolution in frequency.

Convolution of two length-$N$ sequences with the index taken modulo $N$, so what slides off one end wraps round to the other. Multiplying two $N$-point DFTs gives the DFT of the circular convolution, not the linear one.

Ordinary convolution with no wrap-around. Two sequences of lengths $N$ and $M$ give $N + M - 1$ outputs; zero padding both to at least that length makes circular convolution equal to linear convolution.
Appending zeros to a sequence before a DFT. For fast convolution, padding both sequences to length at least $N + M - 1$ leaves room for the whole result, so nothing wraps round.
A way to convolve a long signal with a short filter by FFT: cut the signal into blocks, convolve each block (zero-padded) with the filter, and add the overlapping tails of neighbouring results.
A block method for long convolutions by FFT: take overlapping input blocks, do a circular convolution of each with the filter, and keep only the outputs that wrap-around has not spoiled.

Like convolution but without the flip: $(x \star h)(t) = \int x(\tau)\, h(\tau - t)\, d\tau$ for real signals. It measures how well $h$ matches $x$ at each shift; the layers of convolutional neural networks compute this.
The cross-correlation of a signal with itself. It peaks at zero shift, and its Fourier transform is the energy (or power) spectrum $|X(f)|^2$.
The small array (such as a 3 by 3 grid of weights) that an image or signal is convolved with to blur, sharpen or find edges. It plays the part of the impulse response.
Undoing a convolution: recovering $x$ from $y = x * h$. In frequency it is $X = Y/H$, which blows up noise wherever $|H(f)|$ is small, so in practice it needs regularisation.

A filter whose impulse response is the time-reversed copy of the pulse being looked for, so its output is the cross-correlation of the received signal with that pulse; in white noise it gives the largest signal-to-noise ratio at the pulse's arrival.
A rule $T$ that sends vectors to vectors and respects addition and scaling: $T(au + bv) = aT(u) + bT(v)$. In the plane it is given by a 2×2 matrix whose columns are the images of $e_1$ and $e_2$.
An eigenvalue $\lambda$ together with a matching eigenvector $v \ne 0$, so that $Av = \lambda v$. Any non-zero multiple of $v$ goes with the same $\lambda$.

Writing a matrix as $A = PDP^{-1}$, where the columns of $P$ are eigenvectors and $D$ is diagonal with the eigenvalues. It needs $n$ independent eigenvectors for an $n \times n$ matrix, and it gives $A^k = PD^kP^{-1}$.
Matrices $A$ and $B = Q^{-1}AQ$ for an invertible $Q$: the same linear map written in two bases. They have the same characteristic polynomial, eigenvalues, trace and determinant.
Rewriting vectors and matrices in a different set of basis vectors. If the columns of $P$ are the new basis, coordinates convert by $P^{-1}$, and a matrix $A$ becomes $P^{-1}AP$.
A square matrix with only zeros below its diagonal (upper) or above it (lower). Its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries, and its determinant is their product.

The closed form $F_n = (\varphi^n - \psi^n)/\sqrt5$ for the Fibonacci numbers, where $\varphi = (1+\sqrt5)/2$ and $\psi = (1-\sqrt5)/2$ are the eigenvalues of $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$.
Another name for an eigenvalue: a root of the characteristic polynomial $\det(\lambda I - A)$.

The number $\varphi = (1 + \sqrt5)/2 \approx 1.618$, the larger root of $\lambda^2 = \lambda + 1$. It is the dominant eigenvalue of the Fibonacci matrix, so ratios of consecutive Fibonacci numbers tend to it.

The numbers $0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, \ldots$ with $F_{n+1} = F_n + F_{n-1}$. In matrix form $\begin{pmatrix} F_{n+1} \\ F_n \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} F_n \\ F_{n-1} \end{pmatrix}$.
A square matrix equal to its own transpose, $A^{\top} = A$. A real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and perpendicular eigenvectors, and can be written $A = Q\Lambda Q^{\top}$.
A real square matrix $Q$ whose columns are perpendicular vectors of length 1, so that $Q^{\top}Q = I$ and $Q^{-1} = Q^{\top}$. It turns or flips space without changing lengths or angles.

The number $x^{\top}Ax$ built from a symmetric matrix $A$ and a vector $x$, a sum of terms $a_{ij}x_ix_j$. In coordinates along the eigenvectors it becomes $\lambda_1c_1^2 + \lambda_2c_2^2 + \cdots$ with no cross terms.
A symmetric matrix with $x^{\top}Ax > 0$ for every non-zero $x$. Equivalent: every eigenvalue is positive. Its level curve $x^{\top}Ax = 1$ is an ellipse or ellipsoid.

The perpendicular directions given by the eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix. Measured along them, its quadratic form $x^{\top}Ax$ has no cross terms; they are the axes of the image of the unit circle (half-lengths $|\lambda_i|$) and, for a positive definite matrix, of the ellipse $x^{\top}Ax = 1$ (half-lengths $1/\sqrt{\lambda_i}$).

A matrix that turns the plane by an angle $\theta$ and keeps lengths: $\begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}$. Its eigenvalues are $e^{\pm j\theta}$. In space, a rotation about an axis has the axis as eigenvector for $\lambda = 1$ and trace $1 + 2\cos\theta$.

The pair $a \pm bj$ in which the non-real eigenvalues of a real matrix always occur. The matrix scales by $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ and turns by $\operatorname{atan2}(b, a)$ in the plane spanned by the real and imaginary parts of the eigenvector, measured in the axes those two vectors give.
The number of times an eigenvalue $\lambda_0$ appears as a root of the characteristic polynomial, that is, the power of $(\lambda - \lambda_0)$ in its factorisation.
The dimension of the eigenspace of an eigenvalue: the number of independent eigenvectors it has. It is never larger than the algebraic multiplicity.

A square matrix with one eigenvalue $\lambda$ on the diagonal and 1 on the superdiagonal, such as $\begin{pmatrix} \lambda & 1 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{pmatrix}$. It has a single eigenvector direction, and its powers are $\begin{pmatrix} \lambda^k & k\lambda^{k-1} \\ 0 & \lambda^k \end{pmatrix}$.
The block-diagonal form, made of Jordan blocks, to which every square matrix over the complex numbers is similar. It is diagonal exactly when the matrix has a full set of eigenvectors.

A matrix such as $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ that slides each point sideways by an amount proportional to its distance from a line. Its only eigenvalue is 1 and it has a single eigenvector direction, so it is defective.

A vector $w$ with $(A - \lambda I)w = v$, where $v$ is an eigenvector for $\lambda$ (or, more generally, $(A - \lambda I)^m w = 0$ for some $m$). Chains of them fill the gaps left by a defective matrix and build its Jordan form.

Finding the dominant eigenvector of a matrix $A$ by repeating $w \to Aw/|Aw|$ from almost any starting vector. The direction converges to the eigenvector of the largest-size eigenvalue, with error shrinking like $|\lambda_2/\lambda_1|^k$.

The eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ of largest absolute value, when it is strictly larger in size than all the others. In $A^kv$ its term $c_1\lambda_1^kv_1$ outgrows the rest, so repeated multiplication turns every vector towards its eigenvector.

For a vector $w \ne 0$, the number $\rho(w) = w^{\top}Aw / w^{\top}w$. It equals $\lambda$ when $w$ is an eigenvector, and for a symmetric $A$ it lies between the smallest and largest eigenvalues and is wrong only to second order near an eigenvector.
Power iteration applied to $(A - \mu I)^{-1}$, whose eigenvalues are $1/(\lambda - \mu)$. It converges to the eigenvector whose eigenvalue is nearest the shift $\mu$, and quickly when $\mu$ is close.

A ranking of web pages given by the steady state of a random surfer who follows a link with probability $d$ (usually $0.85$) and jumps to a random page otherwise. It is the eigenvector for $\lambda = 1$ of the column-stochastic matrix $G = dH + (1-d)\,\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}/n$, found by power iteration.

The patterns in which a vibrating system can move with all parts oscillating at one frequency. For $m\,x'' = -kKx$ they are the eigenvectors of $K$, with $\omega = \sqrt{\lambda k/m}$, and any motion is a sum of them.

The standard method for computing all eigenvalues of a matrix: factor $A_k = Q_kR_k$ and form $A_{k+1} = R_kQ_k = Q_k^{\top}A_kQ_k$. The matrices are all similar, and they usually tend to a triangular matrix with the eigenvalues on its diagonal (a complex pair of a real matrix leaves a $2 \times 2$ block).

Every eigenvalue of a square matrix lies in at least one disc in the complex plane centred at a diagonal entry $a_{ii}$ with radius $\sum_{j \ne i}|a_{ij}|$. A group of $m$ discs separate from the rest contains exactly $m$ eigenvalues.
Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation: if $p(\lambda) = \det(\lambda I - A)$ then $p(A) = 0$. For a $2 \times 2$ matrix, $A^2 = (\operatorname{tr}A)A - (\det A)I$.

A linear system $x' = Ax$ is asymptotically stable when every solution tends to $0$, which happens exactly when every eigenvalue of $A$ has negative real part. For $x_{k+1} = Ax_k$ the condition is that every $|\lambda| < 1$.
A matrix with non-negative entries whose columns each add to $1$, so that $p \to Ap$ keeps a probability vector's total at $1$. It always has the eigenvalue $1$ and no eigenvalue larger in size.
The value $L$ that $f(x)$ gets arbitrarily close to as $x$ gets close to $a$ without equalling it. It need not exist, and need not equal $f(a)$.
The value $f(x)$ approaches using only inputs on one side of the point. The two-sided limit exists when both one-sided limits exist and agree.
A function whose limit at each point equals its value there: no holes and no jumps.
The limit of $(f(x+h) - f(x))/h$ as $h$ approaches 0: the rate of change of $f$ at $x$ and the slope of its tangent line.
A straight line through two points of a curve. Its slope is the average rate of change between them.
The derivative of $f(g(x))$ is $f'(g(x))\, g'(x)$: rates of change multiply through a chain of functions.
The derivative of a product: $(fg)' = f'g + fg'$.
A sum of thin rectangle areas, $\sum f(x_i)\, \Delta x$, that approximates an integral and tends to it as the strips narrow.
The number $\int_a^b f(x)\, dx$: the limit of Riemann sums, equal to the signed area between the graph and the axis.
A function $F$ with $F' = f$. On an interval any two differ by a constant.
For continuous $f$ with $F' = f$, $\int_a^b f(x)\, dx = F(b) - F(a)$; and the area function $\int_a^x f(t)\, dt$ has derivative $f(x)$.
The chain rule run backwards: change the variable of integration, along with $dx$ and the limits.
The product rule run backwards: $\int u v' = [uv] - \int u' v$.
An integral over an infinite range, or of an unbounded function, defined as a limit of ordinary integrals. It converges if that limit exists.
A description of a system by a first-order vector equation for its state and an equation for its output, $x' = Ax + Bu$, $y = Cx + Du$. For a system with $n$ states, $A$ is $n \times n$.

One of the $n$ numbers that make up the state vector: together with the input from now on, they fix the future of the system. Typical choices are positions and velocities, capacitor voltages and inductor currents, or tank levels.
The first of the two state-space equations, $x' = Ax + Bu$: it gives the rate of change of the state from the present state and the input.
The second state-space equation, $y = Cx + Du$: it says which combination of the states, plus how much of the input directly, is measured as the output $y$.
The motion of a system started from a state $x(0)$ with the input set to zero: $x(t) = e^{At}x(0)$. It is the part of the solution that comes from the initial state alone.
The motion caused by the input alone, starting from rest: $x(t) = \int_0^t e^{A(t-\tau)}Bu(\tau)\,d\tau$. By superposition it adds to the zero-input response.
The matrix $\Phi(t) = e^{At}$ that carries the state of $x' = Ax$ from time $0$ to time $t$, so that $x(t) = \Phi(t)x(0)$.
The constant output a stable system settles to for a unit constant input: $G(0) = -CA^{-1}B + D$, when $A$ is invertible. A pole at $s = 0$ makes it infinite.
Any state-space model $(A, B, C, D)$ whose transfer function is a given $G(s)$. There are infinitely many, of different sizes and with different states.

The realisation of $G(s) = (b_1s + b_0)/(s^2 + a_1s + a_0)$ with $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -a_0 & -a_1 \end{pmatrix}$, $B = (0, 1)^{\top}$, $C = (b_0, b_1)$: the coefficients of the denominator fill the last row of $A$.

The transposed counterpart of the controllable canonical form: $A$ is the transpose of the companion matrix, the numerator coefficients sit in $B$, and, for $G(s) = (b_1s + b_0)/(s^2 + a_1s + a_0)$, $C = (0, 1)$.

The borderline case in which no motion grows but some do not decay: every eigenvalue has $\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda \le 0$, and those on the imaginary axis are not defective (each has as many independent eigenvectors as its multiplicity, as a simple eigenvalue always does). An undamped oscillator is marginally stable.

The matrix equation $A^{\top}P + PA = -Q$. If it has a positive definite solution $P$ for some positive definite $Q$, then $V = x^{\top}Px$ decreases along every motion and $A$ is asymptotically stable.

The device or model that keeps a sampled input constant between sampling instants, so that $u(t) = u[k]$ for $kT \le t < (k+1)T$. It is what a digital-to-analogue converter does, and it makes the sampled state equation exact: $x[k+1] = \Phi x[k] + \Gamma u[k]$.

The time $T$ between successive samples of a sampled system. A continuous pole $s$ becomes the discrete pole $z = e^{sT}$, so the same plant looks different as $T$ changes: the poles crowd towards $z = 0$ as $T$ grows, and oscillations with $\omega T > \pi$ are aliased.

Turning the continuous state equation $x' = Ax + Bu$ into the discrete one $x[k+1] = \Phi x[k] + \Gamma u[k]$. With a zero-order hold, $\Phi = e^{AT}$ and $\Gamma = \int_0^T e^{A\sigma}\,d\sigma\, B$, exactly; Euler's method $\Phi \approx I + AT$ is a cruder alternative that can be unstable.

A system $x' = Ax + Bu$ is controllable if some input takes the state from zero to any chosen state in finite time. It holds exactly when the controllability matrix $\begin{pmatrix} B & AB & \cdots & A^{n-1}B \end{pmatrix}$ has rank $n$.

A system is observable if the output $y = Cx$ and input over some interval fix the initial state uniquely, so the state can be recovered. It holds exactly when the observability matrix with rows $C, CA, \ldots, CA^{n-1}$ has rank $n$.

The matrix $\mathcal{C} = \begin{pmatrix} B & AB & \cdots & A^{n-1}B \end{pmatrix}$ whose columns span the directions the input can push the state. The system is controllable if its rank is $n$; Ackermann's formula uses its inverse.

The matrix $\mathcal{O}$ whose rows are $C, CA, \ldots, CA^{n-1}$, so that, with no input, $(y, y', \ldots) = \mathcal{O}x$ at one instant. The system is observable if its rank is $n$. It is the transpose of the controllability matrix of the dual pair $(A^{\top}, C^{\top})$.
The test that a system is controllable (observable) if and only if its controllability (observability) matrix has full rank $n$. It needs only matrix products and a rank computation.

A mode of a state-space model that is missing from the transfer function: one the input cannot excite (not controllable) or the output cannot see (not observable). It appears as a pole that cancels against a zero in $G(s)$.

aliases: cancellation of a pole and a zero
definition: A pole and a zero of $G(s)$ at the same place, which remove each other from the transfer function. In a state-space model it signals a mode that is uncontrollable or unobservable, and if that mode is unstable the cancellation hides a real danger.

aliases: minimal realisation of a transfer function
definition: A state-space model of a transfer function with the fewest possible states. A realisation is minimal if and only if it is controllable and observable, and then the number of states equals the degree of the reduced denominator of $G(s)$.
A system is stabilisable if every uncontrollable mode is already stable, so that state feedback can make the whole system stable even though it cannot place every pole.
A system is detectable if every unobservable mode is stable. The unseen part then dies away by itself and an observer still converges, only not faster than that mode's own decay.
A control law $u = -Kx + r$ that multiplies the measured state by a gain matrix $K$. The closed loop is $x' = (A - BK)x + Br$, so choosing $K$ moves the poles to the eigenvalues of $A - BK$.
Choosing the feedback gain $K$ so that $A - BK$ has chosen eigenvalues. Possible for any set of poles (in conjugate pairs) exactly when the system is controllable.

The gain $K = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \cdots & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\mathcal{C}^{-1}\varphi(A)$ that places the poles of $A - BK$ at the roots of the polynomial $\varphi$, for a controllable single-input system with controllability matrix $\mathcal{C}$.
A closed loop feeds a measured quantity, such as the state, back to choose the input; an open loop applies an input chosen in advance. With state feedback the closed-loop matrix is $A - BK$.
The scalar $N = 1/\big(C(BK - A)^{-1}B\big)$ in $u = -Kx + Nr$ that makes the steady-state output equal the reference $r$, since feedback alone usually changes the steady-state gain.
A sampled-data design that places all closed-loop poles at $z = 0$, so that the state reaches zero in at most $n$ samples. It needs large gains and large control effort.

A model $\hat{x}' = A\hat{x} + Bu + L(y - C\hat{x})$ run alongside the plant to estimate its state from the input and the measured output. The error $e = x - \hat{x}$ obeys $e' = (A - LC)e$, so $L$ sets how fast the estimate converges.
The gain $L$ that multiplies the output error $y - C\hat{x}$ in an observer. It is found by pole placement on the dual pair $(A^{\top}, C^{\top})$.

For a linear system with a correct model, state feedback $u = -K\hat{x}$ using an observer has the closed-loop poles of $A - BK$ together with those of $A - LC$, so the feedback and the observer can be designed independently.

The pair $(A, C)$ is observable if and only if $(A^{\top}, C^{\top})$ is controllable. Anything designed for controllability, such as pole placement, therefore carries over to observability, which is how observer gains are found.

An observer whose gain $L$ is computed from the strength of the model noise and the measurement noise (through a Riccati equation) so that the estimate has the least error variance among linear estimators.

Writing the state as a sum of modes, $x(t) = \sum_i c_i e^{\lambda_i t} v_i$, one for each eigenvalue $\lambda_i$ and eigenvector $v_i$ of $A$; in the eigenvector coordinates $A$ becomes diagonal and each mode evolves on its own.
A system whose modes decay at very different rates: the fast modes die away first and the state then moves slowly along the line or plane of the slow modes, which dominate the response.
Replacing a system by one with fewer states that gives nearly the same response, for example by keeping the dominant (slowest) poles and replacing each fast mode by its steady-state gain.
A test on the coefficients of a polynomial for all its roots to lie in the left half-plane, without finding them; for $s^3 + a_2s^2 + a_1s + a_0$ it is $a_2, a_1, a_0 > 0$ and $a_2a_1 > a_0$.
